claims.text: A process is one run of a program: the operating system — the program that starts other programs and keeps track of them — gives that run its own memory, at least one flow of execution through the instructions, and a number that names it while it lasts.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Threads and threading ("A process is an executing program"; the OS gives processor time to its threads); Garbage collection fundamentals ("its own, separate virtual address space")

claims.text: A process id identifies a run while that run is alive, and the system may hand the same number to a later run.
claims.source_hint: dotnet API reference, System.Diagnostics.Process.Id, Remarks ("Process identifiers can be reused by the system")

claims.text: The exit-code convention is 0 for success and any other value for failure, though a run stopped from outside can leave a nonzero number without having failed.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Main() return values ("0 usually means success, and a nonzero value means there's an error"); for the second half, the 143 in outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/list-processes.txt

claims.text: Running a file on disk asks the operating system to create a process for that run, with memory that only that run can reach.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Garbage collection fundamentals, virtual memory section ("Each process has its own, separate virtual address space")

claims.text: Two runs of the same file get separate memory and separate ids, and neither can read the other's memory unless it asks the operating system for something built for sharing.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Garbage collection fundamentals (separate virtual address space) and Memory-mapped files (non-persisted files "suitable for creating shared memory for inter-process communications")

claims.text: scripts/up.sh finishes and returns the terminal while the processes it started keep running.
claims.source_hint: Docker docs, detached mode (`docker compose up -d`); examples/don-hang/scripts/up.sh at stage-0, then `docker compose ps`

claims.text: A run usually ends in one of three ways: it ends by itself (its main function returns, or it asks to end), it crashes, or something outside it stops it.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Main() and command-line arguments ("When Main returns, the program ends"); Exceptions in managed threads ("the unhandled exception causes the application to terminate"); Environment.Exit

claims.text: When a run is stopped from outside and does nothing about the stop, the number reported for it is not one the program chose.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: `sleep 30 & kill $!; wait $!` reports 143 while the program itself returns nothing; outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/list-processes.txt:4

claims.text: Process.GetCurrentProcess().Id is the number the operating system assigned to the current run, and the kind of tool that lists runs lists it under the same number.
claims.source_hint: dotnet API reference, Process.Id, Remarks ("the process identifier uniquely identifies the process throughout the system"); run the sample and match against `ps`

claims.text: Environment.ProcessPath is the path of the executable that started this run, so it is the same on every run started the same way, while the id changes.
claims.source_hint: dotnet API reference, System.Environment.ProcessPath ("Returns the path of the executable that started the currently executing process") and its Remarks on renamed or deleted executables

claims.text: Environment.CurrentDirectory is the folder the current run works in.
claims.source_hint: dotnet API reference, System.Environment.CurrentDirectory ("the fully qualified path of the current working directory")

claims.text: `sleep` is a program that stays alive for the number of seconds given to it, so `sleep 30` can still be listed a moment after it starts.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: `sleep 30 &` then `ps -p $!` lists it; the captured output shows both copies. Behaviour of lab/Dockerfile's image; no version key covers it (open_questions)

claims.text: In the script, `&` lets it start a program and carry on without waiting, so both `sleep 30` runs are alive at the same time.
claims.source_hint: scripts/computer/list-processes.sh:7-13 at stage-0: the echo prints without waiting out two 30-second sleeps, and `ps` then lists both. No version key covers the shell (open_questions)

claims.text: The script stops both copies the same way and reports an ending number for the first one only.
claims.source_hint: scripts/computer/list-processes.sh:15-17 at stage-0 (`kill` on both, then `wait "$second" ... || true`) and outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/list-processes.txt:4, which carries one ending line

claims.text: Commands inside `( … )` run as a separate run of the script itself, not a program on disk, so `( exit 3 )` ends that run with the number 3.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/scripts/computer/list-processes.sh:20-21 at stage-0 and its captured output. No version key covers the shell (see open_questions)

claims.text: The captured output of list-processes.sh reports 143 for the copy stopped from outside, then 0 and 3 for the two endings the script chose.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/list-processes.txt at stage-0

claims.text: The ids of the two sleep copies change on every run, which is why the captured output file masks them as "...".
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/outputs/unstable.regex at stage-0 (pid pattern) plus two consecutive runs of scripts/computer/list-processes.sh

claims.text: Each run of a program starts with its own memory, so a second run does not see values the first run held.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Garbage collection fundamentals ("Each process has its own, separate virtual address space")

claims.text: A process can be running and answering while printing nothing, so silence does not mean it has stopped.
claims.source_hint: Docker docs, detached mode; examples/don-hang at stage-0: after scripts/up.sh returns, the site keeps answering with no further output

claims.text: A failing run's exit code changes nothing for its caller unless something reads that number.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Main() return values ("your program can send status information to other programs or scripts that run the executable"); the behaviour is the caller's, and versions.yaml pins no shell

claims.text: Running list-processes.sh twice almost always gives four different ids, and gives the same three ending numbers, 143, 0 and 3, both times.
claims.source_hint: Two consecutive runs of examples/don-hang/scripts/computer/list-processes.sh at stage-0; Process.Id Remarks on identifier reuse explain why "almost always" and not "always"

claims.text: A run that crashes does not choose the number reported for it either.
claims.source_hint: dotnet docs, Exceptions in managed threads ("the unhandled exception causes the application to terminate") — the runtime sets the code; contrast Environment.Exit, where the program gives it

claims.text: At stage-0, the site that answers the browser is served by one long-lived process, and it is not the API of Đơn Hàng, which does not exist at this tag.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/docker-compose.yml at stage-0: service `web` (image caddy:2.10.0) serving www/, and no API service anywhere in the file; `docker compose ps` after scripts/up.sh

claims.text: A second run of a program can fail while the first is still running, when the first holds something only one run at a time can have.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/docker-compose.yml at stage-0 publishes 8080 and 8443 on the lab box; a second listener asking for the same port is refused (address already in use). Docker docs, Compose ports

open_questions: One technical major is still open and cannot be closed from this session: the C# block quotes `Process.GetCurrentProcess().Id`, which CA1837 flags as a suggestion on .NET 10, and the sample never disposes the Process instance. Fixing it means editing HelloProcess.cs in examples/don-hang at tag stage-0 — a change to the example repository, which CLAUDE.md rule 1 reserves for the owner (prompt 08), and stage-0 is already tagged and quoted by an approved lesson. Until the owner decides, the block stays verbatim and this lesson cannot reach `approved`. See repo_changes_needed.

The shell and `ps` behaviour behind claims 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 22 is pinned by the lab image in examples/don-hang/lab/Dockerfile, but content/versions.yaml has no key for a shell or for procps. An image bump would silently invalidate section 5 with no version key to trigger the re-review that versions.yaml policy requires. The technical review asks for a `shell` key (check: `bash --version`) and optionally `procps`; that is a change to a source-of-truth file, so it needs the owner's decision. Until then every number in section 5 and in Try it carries the hedge that it is what the example system reports.

Claim 21 stayed `unverified` in the technical review: no source in versions.yaml governs what a caller does with an exit code nobody reads, because versions.yaml pins no shell. The sentence is kept at the level of principle ("unless something reads that number") and asserts nothing about a particular caller.

Outline item 3 says a process ends when its main function returns, when it crashes, or when the OS kills it. The lesson states all three but adds "usually", because the reviewer found no source making the list exhaustive and the docs' own samples end a run with `Environment.Exit`.

repo_changes_needed.need: In HelloProcess.cs, replace `var process = System.Diagnostics.Process.GetCurrentProcess();` plus `process.Id` with a single `Console.WriteLine($"process id: {Environment.ProcessId}");`. CA1837 is a default suggestion on .NET 10 against GetCurrentProcess().Id, and the Process instance the sample creates is never disposed, so a junior copying the file writes code their own build flags. The lesson now quotes lines 8-13, so the quoted range and the sentence introducing it would need updating with the change.
